---
title: "Deep Neural Networks for Mortality Prediction from EHR Vital-Sign Time Series"
---

::: {.project-meta}
Research project · University of Nevada, Las Vegas · June – July 2025 · Team of four ("Deep Patient") · Faculty: Dr. Mingon Kang
:::

A team research project carried out during a summer research program at the
University of Nevada, Las Vegas, predicting patient mortality from short
sequences of routinely recorded vital signs. The practical obstacle in this data
is that vital signs are not recorded on a regular schedule: the interval between
measurements varies from patient to patient, so the series must be placed on a
common time grid before any sequence model can be applied. The project was
designed around that choice — two interpolation schemes crossed with two network
architectures, compared on the same cohort.

## Data

Electronic health records from a cancer center in Brazil. Static features (age,
sex, ICU admission status), six vital signs — heart rate, respiratory rate,
blood pressure, oxygen saturation, body temperature and blood glucose — observed
at five consecutive time points (*t* through *t*−4) for 30 time-varying features,
plus delta features encoding the change in each vital sign between successive
points. The outcome was patient mortality, coded as survived or deceased. After
preprocessing, the analysis set comprised 1,682 patients per class, reshaped to
16,820 × 7 across the five time steps.

## Methods

Irregular measurement intervals were resolved by interpolating onto the median
observed interval, using either linear or non-linear interpolation. Each
interpolation was paired with a convolutional network and with an LSTM, giving a
2 × 2 comparison; features were standardized and the classes were balanced. My
assignment within the team was the linear-interpolation + LSTM arm. Models were
compared on F1 score, with accuracy and AUC reported alongside, and training
length was set by the epoch at which validation loss began to rise.

## Findings

The convolutional models outperformed the recurrent ones on every metric.

| Configuration | Accuracy | F1 | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|
| CNN, linear interpolation | 0.773 | 0.762 | 0.853 |
| CNN, non-linear interpolation | 0.765 | 0.761 | 0.834 |
| LSTM, non-linear interpolation | 0.684 | 0.656 | 0.744 |
| LSTM, linear interpolation | 0.671 | 0.638 | 0.735 |

: Best result per configuration {.striped tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

Interpolation scheme mattered far less than architecture: within each
architecture the two interpolation methods differed by roughly one point of F1.
The comparison is limited to a single cohort, and external validation on an
independent dataset was identified as the necessary next step rather than
completed.
